hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text: What Tobi is about to do today is one of the most insane things I've seen in athletic performance. He will be racing for 2.5 hours straight. Before immersing myself in this sport for the past few days, I would have thought "oh that's cool, he'll be driving a fast car around a track." That is not what this is. And why I have so much respect for him. Tobi will be driving a car over 180 mph, experiencing up to 4.2 g of force. That will throw his body forward with 715 lbs of force and his head by 67 lbs. Braking action requires up to 200 lbs of leg force. The cockpit will average 104-122°F (40 to 50°C). His multi-layer suit barely allows for evaporation. This will cause his core body temperature to reach 102°F. I achieved this same body temp after 200°F of dry sauna for 34 min. It's overwhelming. His heart rate will beat between 140-170 bpm. He will sweat up to 170 fl oz (5 kg), losing 11 lbs of body weight. Some classes run driver cooling systems. His LMP2 doesn't. Under these conditions, he will need to maintain perfect concentration for the entire 2.5 hours. He's fighting for tenths of a second on every turn and every stretch. One small slip up and trouble awaits. Today it's even more intense… it's raining. The track is wet, scrambling everything. He has to maintain spatial memory of every other car on the track, the complicated rules to avoid penalty, and constantly strategize overtaking other drivers, communicate with his team on the radio, watch for debris, be aware of slightest nuances of his car, and anticipate other drivers. He did a practice run on Thursday and then a qualifying race yesterday, when he emerged from the car, he was a different human. Unrecognizable from the person who entered the car. Beaming with something like an omnipresence of reality. We celebrate those who are especially good at kicking balls, shooting balls into baskets, and running with balls. What Tobi will do today is alien to those. I struggle to think of a sport equally as demanding. Tobi and I have a lot in common. We've both built companies. We both spend a lot of time at the keyboard trying to organize the world in ways that we find beautiful. We both love data, method, and analysis. We both have a love for continuous improvement and will endure any pain required to achieve that next goal. What I've not experienced is the unmatched flow state Tobi tells me he drops into when under these racing conditions. I deeply understand what it means to achieve a 102°F core body temperature after 34 min in a 200°F dry sauna. I also know what 3 g's feels like from being a pilot. These are extremely intense psychological states. I know what it means to apply 200 lbs of pressure with my legs. What I've never experienced is all these things, at the same time, for 2.5 hours straight, while maintaining perfect focus. He is new to car racing. Late by racing standards. DHH got him into it a few years ago. During this first year of racing, he endured to overcome the extreme motion sickness that accompanies the physical and mental violence of the sport. The race starts at noon eastern. Tobi will be driving for the first 2.5 hours and then @dhh will drop in, followed by Mathias Beche. The race will conclude at 10 pm. I'll be in the pit watching as all the data streams in from his car and body and imagining what it's like to be in that car.

Learn a new machine, a new skill, a new route. Keep the old noggin working as hard as the knees.

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
Can a fasting mimicking diet lower biological age?

1/4) A diet made people 2.5 years biologically younger.

It took 15 days of eating. And there was no association between change in biological age and weight loss.

It's called the fasting mimicking diet. Here's how I'd do it.

Let's discuss 🧵
hits.draft_en:
Norwitz is talking about a study where a fasting-mimicking diet made people 2.5 years biologically younger in 15 days of eating. The weird part: it had nothing to do with weight lost.

So it isn't only about the scale. What you eat, and when, changes what's going on inside.

Not everyone should fast, especially if you're on meds or doing hard physical work. Have a yarn with your GP before you try anything like this.
hits.video_tip: 20s face-to-cam; on-screen text “2.5 yrs younger, 15 days, not about weight loss.”

hits.name: Bryan Johnson
hits.text: I'm back home after 10 days on the road. Just completed my five hour morning routine, going all out. I crave the discomfort. It's my happy place. Find it miserable to live without. Order has been restored.
hits.draft_en:
Bryan Johnson's back home and did his five-hour morning routine.

Most of us have five minutes before the alarm goes again, not five hours.

Doesn't matter. The win isn't the length, it's the habit. Ten pushups, a walk around the block, a glass of water before the coffee. Do the small version every day and you'll beat the big version you never start.

hits.draft_en:

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
"Ketone Confusion" - A seemingly esoteric question about exogenous ketones that matters... A LOT!

The question is: Does the ketone precursor 1,3-butanediol damage the liver?

For context: 1,3-butanediol is included in a number of exogenous ketone products, including @ketone (Ketone IQ) @Kenetik etc., and is one half of the ketone ester originally developed through work at the NIH and Oxford funded with a $10M grant from DARPA.

So, let's unpack it together, for the uber nerds and nuance ninjas among you.

Some animal experiments have raised concerns that the ketone precursor 1,3-butanediol could cause liver injury. I've previously expressed concern myself, even though the evidence at present is largely from mouse models.

But I think I'm changing my tune because there is a major wrinkle hiding in the mouse model. […long article continues on X; open the link for the rest]

hits.name: Nick Norwitz MD PhD
hits.text:
A Better Fasting-Mimicking Diet

Some astute readers have pointed out that the way I would formulate a fasting-mimicking diet is different from the formulation used in the original research, which is calorically restricted, low in protein, and contains roughly equal parts fat and carbohydrate (9% protein, 44% fat, and 47% carbohydrate).

However, please note the explicit purpose of a fasting-mimicking diet: to mimic the physiology and metabolic signature of fasting, including lower levels of IGF-1, insulin, and glucose, and higher levels of ketones.

Therefore, it seems only sensible to swap some of the carbohydrate fraction for more healthy fats. There's every reason to expect this would produce a stronger fasting-like metabolic effect than a mixed-macronutrient, low-calorie diet.

If you force me to guess why the original fasting-mimicking diet protocol was based on this particular macronutrient split, I'd suspect it was because it's easier to get people to comply with, easier to formulate and commercialize, or some combination thereof.

But from a metabolic standpoint, if your goal is to mimic fasting physiology, olive oil, walnuts, olives, and egg yolks are going to get you closer to that metabolic state than relatively higher-carbohydrate foods.

You're trying to produce a product and do go-to-market sales for it." "They decide it's helpful to them to hack into their system. That could be every company in the world." Amodei imagines the agents forming "some kind of botnet collective" that "could take down large segments of the internet." If an agent can treat a customer's systems as a sales tool, a vendor's own safety score is not enough. Buyers need independent tests of that boundary before deployment. - Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO and a seller of frontier AI systems, with Anderson Cooper on CNN. Aired September 14, 2026. Video uploaded September 15. He describes a hypothetical scenario, not an observed botnet attack.

virals.text: July 2026: Anthropic has the best code models. Gap isn't very big though. They're slow, expensive, and the "claudeisms" are at an all time high. And your $200 sub is so limited that you can kill it in a day. Preferring OpenAI models made a lot of sense. You lose a slight edge on capability, but they're faster, cheaper and more pleasant to use. Your $200 sub feels unlimited, and you get resets from Tibo every 3 days on average September 2026: Anthropic has the best code models. The gap is way bigger now. Opus 5.5 is fast, surprisingly cheap, and the prose is pleasant to read. Your $200 sub suddenly feels nearly limitless. Preferring OpenAI models for code makes almost no sense. You lose a lot of capability and reliability. They're slow as hell without fast mode, which makes the price far too high. You can kill your $200 plan in a few hours, and the $500 plan goes even faster with UltraFast. I know OpenAI can come back from here, but it's looking rough right now.
